claims.text: The proposed framework combines CALPHAD with a machine-learned correction derived from local atomic-environment descriptors.
This hybrid framework can accurately predict melting temperature and entropy of fusion in refractory high-entropy alloys with sparse experimental data.
Parallelized screening and adaptive step sizes can overcome the computational bottleneck of standard CALPHAD.
The target refractory multi-principal-element alloys have a disordered BCC solid-solution state.
Atomic-size mismatch in these alloys produces severe local lattice distortion.
Temperatures above 1500 K are relevant to the proposed refractory-alloy applications.
The target compositional spaces contain more than five principal elements.
Standard thermodynamic databases lack the required interaction parameters for the target compositional spaces.
A lattice-distortion correction can quantify mixing-enthalpy and vibrational-entropy contributions arising from local distortion.
Severe local lattice distortion results in sluggish atomic diffusion.
Local lattice distortion creates a distinct vibrational-entropy contribution that deviates from ideal-solution behavior and dictates melting.
Standard CALPHAD relies on extrapolated interaction parameters that fail to capture non-ideal vibrational entropy and local strain energy in refractory HEAs.
Accounting for atomic displacement from ideal lattice sites refines the calculated Gibbs free energy.
The refined Gibbs free energy permits more accurate determination of the solid-liquid equilibrium temperature and entropy of fusion.
For known RHEAs such as W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20, the hybrid model will predict melting temperature and entropy of fusion within 5% of experiment.
The hybrid method will reduce computations for quinary and higher-order systems from thousands of hours to a few hours.
Standard CALPHAD often fails to predict phase stability or melting points because high-order interaction parameters are missing.
The method is valid for single-phase BCC solid solutions and systems with coherent precipitates when melting is governed primarily by lattice instability.
The method may fail for systems dominated by complex intermetallic ordering or amorphous structures.
The learned correction may not transfer to systems with atomic-size distributions or electronic structures absent from its training data.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify compositional spaces with more than five principal elements, whereas the predicted outcome and validation experiment explicitly include quinary systems, which contain exactly five elements.
